newsitem.title: USA: Administration opposes Republican toxic waste plan.
newsitem.headline: Administration opposes Republican toxic waste plan.

text.p: The Clinton administration said Wednesday it opposed a Senate Republican proposal to reform the programme for cleaning up the nation's worst toxic waste sites, continuing a two-year-old stalemate.
Lawmakers and the administration are eager to overhaul the multibillion-dollar Superfund programme, which has been slow to clean up dumps that were used for hazardous waste.
In his State of the Union Address, President Bill Clinton emphasised that one in four Americans lives within four miles of a toxic dump and vowed to double the pace of cleanups.
But in her first public comments on the latest Republican plan, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Carol Browner raised serious concerns and urged senators to craft a bill from scratch.

"Rather than build on the proven successes of our administrative reforms, (the bill) would impose a new system that could unfortunately result in delay in cleanups, (and) shift costs from polluters to taxpayers," she said.
"Overall, S.8 would create a system that is less protective of the public's health than the one we have today," she told the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.
"Why don't we pull out a blank sheet of paper and draft a Superfund reform bill that recognises the progress we've made," she added.

Over the last four years the EPA has taken steps to speed up cleanups, completing work at 250 Superfund sites. Work at some of those sites had begun more than 10 years ago. There are more than 1,300 sites on the Superfund list.

One of the thorniest issues dividing Republicans and the administration, states say polluters should be held responsible for cleanup costs, and not be let off the hook, as some Republicans have proposed.

"We do not let responsible parties walk away from polluted sites, leaving the problem for taxpayers to solve," Gov. Christine Todd Whitman of New Jersey, the state with the most Superfund sites, said at a House Transportation subcommittee hearing Wednesday.
States are also pressing Washington to give them more authority to run Superfund cleanups, which they say they can do more efficiently than the federal government.
